newsitem.title: FRANCE: France to vote as Chirac gambles presidency.
newsitem.headline: France to vote as Chirac gambles presidency.

text.p: France votes on Sunday in the first round of parliamentary elections that will either renew support for conservative President Jacques Chirac or condemn him to rule in awkward tandem with leftwingers.

Calling the snap poll, Chirac said France needed a "new elan" to join a single European currency from a position of strength and opinion polls before a blackout last weekend suggested his centre-right allies were likely to retain power for the next five years.

The Paris bourse, where secret polls are a factor driving prices, ended only 0.77 percent lower last week. Most investors apparently bet that Chirac's gamble would work and he would not be forced into an uneasy "cohabitation" with the Socialist-led left.

France's 39 million electors vote between 8 a.m. (0600 GMT) and 8 p.m. (1800 GMT) for the 577-seat National Assembly. Run-off contests will be held on June 1 in those constituencies where no candidate wins an absolute majority.

A total of 6,389 candidates, including a record 1,469 women on a day coinciding with Mothers' Day in France, were standing. Weather was forecast to be sunny in the north with partly cloudy skies in the south and some scattered rain.

First results, and pollsters' predictions of the overall winners in a week's time, were due immediately after polling booths closed. Prime Minister Alain Juppe has cautioned that the initial results may be hard to interpret.
Pollsters say many people may abstain following a lacklustre campaign dominated by personality clashes and arguments over record unemployment, austerity measures and European Union integration.

The poll, called by Chirac 10 months early and two years into his own seven-year term, failed to excite voters though they were offered a choice between the cautious free-market economic approach of Chirac's ally Juppe and leftist job creation plans.

Juppe said he would maintain austerity to qualify for a single European currency. He promised a public spending freeze, tax cuts, an accelerated privatisation programme and a reduction in the civil service to give more scope for private initiative.

The Socialist and Communist opposition said it would tackle reord 12.8 percent unemployment, the highest in the Group of Seven industrial nations, by creating 700,000 youth jobs and cutting the work week to 35 hours from 39 without loss of pay.

Socialist leader Lionel Jospin ruled out any more austerity measures to qualify for the euro from 1999 and he imposed conditions on joining, such as the participation of Italy and Spain from the outset.

Chirac warned voters that a period of enforced "cohabitation" with the left could weaken France's voice abroad. But he also said he would not resign even if Jospin became prime minister, making the president a virtual lame duck until 2002.

France had two periods of cohabitation under the late Socialist president Francois Mitterrand, who was forced to govern with Chirac, as premier from 1986-88, and with conservative prime minister Edouard Balladur from 1993-95.
In general, French foreign policy ran smoothly on both occasions.

Analysts said the combined left looked set to win the highest first-round score but would lose to the centre-right on June 1. They said most voters of the far-right National Front would switch to conservatives in the run-offs.

The governing coalition had an overwhelming majority in the outgoing assembly with 464 deputies to 63 Socialists or allies, 24 Communists, 23 independents, two unaffiliated deputies and one vacant seat.
